title: AI can prove theorems, but it still can't ask questions worth asking
dek: University of Toronto mathematician Daniel Litt says models are best at applying known techniques to their limit, but the real value of mathematics is understanding — and understanding still lives in human brains.
why: An honest calibration of AI's mathematical ability from a working mathematician: which results genuinely changed his mind, and which are just headlines. High information density, for anyone who wants an insider's judgment.
who: Engineers and researchers who need a read on AI's mathematical ability, and technical decision-makers who want to know where models are actually strong and where they're weak.
skip: The last ten minutes cover his daughter learning math and an icosahedron toy, unrelated to the main argument.

points.h: The result that changed his mind most is the unit distance problem
points.body: Daniel says his favorite fully autonomous AI result so far is the solution to the Erdős unit distance problem, announced around mid-May. He values it because the result is somewhat creative: it borrows techniques from classic ideas from the 1960s, but those techniques were new to people studying planar point configurations. And it proved productive afterward — a group of mathematicians took these ideas and constructed counterexamples to other open problems, such as the sum-product conjecture over the reals. He calls it the only autonomous result he knows of that, in hindsight, genuinely produced new understanding.

points.h: The model's chain of thought looks very human
points.body: The host asks whether this is "non-human" logical reasoning, and Daniel pushes back: he thinks the argument is very human. Some of the chains of thought OpenAI has released look completely recognizable to him — if he imagined his own chain of thought while solving a problem, it would probably look like that. He says this is true of most results he has studied: there's no brilliant "move 37," it's just a human mathematician doing human mathematics. The only way the model seems non-human is that it never gets tired and knows a lot.

points.h: The claim that math is verifiable is overrated
points.body: Daniel says many people argue math is a verifiable domain, so AI progresses fast there. But his judgment is that models are mainly extending informal reasoning, not Lean proofs, so these techniques will very likely generalize to other fields. He also points out that a lot of mathematical training data doesn't reflect how mathematicians think — papers are polished, textbooks almost never show motivation, so to keep up with a research direction you usually have to talk to the researchers directly.

points.h: Models are strong at applying known techniques, weak at intuition
points.body: Daniel says model results have a fixed flavor: they rely on long computation, or they stitch together technical ideas from many fields and many papers. But they are weaker at intuition and the big picture. He describes how he works: first he has a very non-rigorous philosophy, a sense that this thing is analogous to that thing, and then he works to make it precise. In the best model results so far, he sees little of that kind of reasoning. He stresses that being very good at applying all known techniques is itself powerful, and some mathematicians do high-quality work that way, but that's only a narrow band of what mathematicians care about.

points.h: When humans can't prove it, a better theorem comes out
points.body: Daniel tells the story of his only paper where a model was useful. There was a lemma he wanted to prove, and every frontier model failed to prove it. So he worked through a bunch of examples himself, realized there might be a better statement, and once he found it the model proved that better version quickly. He says that if you now hand the original lemma to ChatGPT 5.6 Pro, it outputs the worst proof you've ever seen — ten pages of brutal computation, zero insight. The proof itself isn't wrong, but it won't lead to this prettier conceptual explanation. He says he realized the ugly proof would work, but he just couldn't bring himself to do it, so he went looking for another argument.

points.h: Current incentives are mass-producing junk papers
points.body: Daniel says the goal of mathematics is not to produce papers, it's to produce understanding. But the current incentive structure doesn't encourage people to really commit. He describes an experiment: have Codex go online, find five recent conjectures in algebraic geometry and prove them, and after a few rounds, within an hour you get three terrible but correct papers, which now sit on his hard drive. He says submissions to arXiv have exploded, much of it obviously low quality, even the same proof of the same theorem appearing three to five times within days. He thinks this isn't necessarily a problem that goes away as models get better.

points.h: A thousand mathematicians, or one mathematician copied a thousand times
points.body: Daniel says mathematical progress comes from letting a thousand flowers bloom, people following their own curiosity, the frontier of knowledge expanding in a relatively even way, and then applications appearing opportunistically. What worries him: if mathematical exploration is subordinated to what models want to pursue, what you get may be one mathematician copied a thousand times, rather than a million mathematicians doing a million different things. The host adds that if the proofs labs put out all converge on similar things, because they technically depend on the same body of literature, then it's unclear where that diversity intuition would come from.

points.h: Model proofs are short because they can't check long ones
points.body: Some people praise model proofs for being short and beautiful, but Daniel's judgment is the opposite: they don't produce long, complex proofs because they can't — their ability to check correctness isn't good enough. He says even when you have a model write a short proof, if you then ask it whether it's right, it often says no. The problem with long proofs is that the model may not know it's wrong. He gives an example: ten problems OpenAI recently released were all formalized in Lean, which is strong evidence they're true; he has no doubt there are more that can't be formalized, because the prerequisite lemmas aren't in Mathlib yet. He also mentions someone posting an 800-page AI-generated proof of resolution of singularities, and says there's no way it's correct.

The largest library of formalized mathematical theorems in the Lean ecosystem; prerequisite lemmas must be in it before a new proof can be formalized.
A classic problem about how often unit distances occur among planar point configurations, long believed to have an upper bound, later overturned by a counterexample.
A conjecture over the reals that addition and multiplication cannot both keep a set small, later refuted by a construction.
A classic theorem in algebraic geometry turning singular varieties into smooth ones, long unresolved in full generality in positive characteristic.
